claim: Burkholderia thailandensis uses acyl-homoserine lactone-mediated quorum sensing systems to regulate hundreds of genes.
source: Burkholderia thailandensis uses acyl-homoserine lactone-mediated quorum sensing systems to regulate hundreds of genes.
evidence: This is a general statement about B. thailandensis QS systems supported by the authors' research and established knowledge in the field.

claim: Cell-cell contact-dependent type VI secretion (T6S) toxin-immunity systems are activated by quorum sensing in B. thailandensis.
source: Here we show that cell-cell contact-dependent type VI secretion (T6S) toxin-immunity systems are among those activated by quorum sensing in B. thailandensis.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: T6S is required to constrain proliferation of quorum sensing mutants in colony cocultures of a BtaR1 quorum-sensing signal receptor mutant and its parent.
source: We also demonstrate that T6S is required to constrain proliferation of quorum sensing mutants in colony cocultures of a BtaR1 quorum-sensing signal receptor mutant and its parent.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated through experimental coculture data.

claim: The BtaR1 mutant is not constrained by and outcompetes its parent in broth coculture, presumably because no cell contact occurs and there is a metabolic cost associated with quorum sensing gene activation.
source: However, the BtaR1 mutant is not constrained by and outcompetes its parent in broth coculture, presumably because no cell contact occurs and there is a metabolic cost associated with quorum sensing gene activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing BtaR1 mutant outcompetes parent in broth, with speculation about the mechanism.

claim: The increased fitness of the wild type over the BtaR1 mutant during agar surface growth is dependent on an intact T6SS-1 apparatus.
source: The increased fitness of the wild type over the BtaR1 mutant during agar surface growth is dependent on an intact T6SS-1 apparatus.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing wild type and T6SS-1 mutants in agar surface competitions.

claim: Quorum sensing activates B. thailandensis T6SS-1 growth inhibition and this control serves to police and constrain quorum-sensing mutants.
source: Thus, quorum sensing activates B. thailandensis T6SS-1 growth inhibition and this control serves to police and constrain quorum-sensing mutants.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: This work defines a novel role for T6SSs in intraspecies mutant control.
source: This work defines a novel role for T6SSs in intraspecies mutant control.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of the study and comparison to existing knowledge about T6SS functions.

claim: AHLs are made by members of the LuxI family of signal synthases.
source: AHLs are made by members of the LuxI family of signal synthases.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about AHL quorum sensing systems.

claim: AHLs can diffuse in and out of cells.
source: The AHLs can diffuse in and out of cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the physical properties of AHL molecules.

claim: At sufficient cell densities, the AHLs accumulate to concentrations needed for expression of specific genes by binding signal receptors of the LuxR family of transcriptional regulators.
source: At sufficient cell densities, the AHLs accumulate to concentrations needed for expression of specific genes by binding signal receptors of the LuxR family of transcriptional regulators (for reviews of QS see (Fuqua et al., 1996)).
evidence: This is established knowledge about AHL quorum sensing mechanisms, supported by citation.

claim: In some bacterial species, QS controls just a few genes and in others it controls hundreds of genes.
source: In some bacterial species, QS controls just a few genes and in others it controls hundreds of genes.
evidence: This is general knowledge about the variability of QS regulons across bacterial species.

claim: Genes for production of secreted or excreted products are overrepresented in AHL quorum sensing regulons.
source: Genes for production of secreted or excreted products are overrepresented in AHL quorum sensing regulons.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the composition of QS regulons.

claim: Extracellular products controlled by QS have at least in some cases been shown to serve as public goods.
source: These extracellular products have at least in some cases been shown to serve as public goods.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the nature of QS-controlled products.

claim: Any member of a group can benefit from the public good regardless of whether that individual has contributed its share of the good.
source: Any member of a group can benefit from the public good regardless of whether that individual has contributed its share of the good (West et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a definition of public goods supported by citation.

claim: There is a metabolic cost associated with QS and QS-activation of gene expression.
source: There is a metabolic cost associated with QS and QS-activation of gene expression.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the costs of QS systems.

claim: QS signal receptor mutants have a fitness advantage over the wild type when growth is on milk protein as the sole carbon and energy source in Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
source: Because QS activates production of extracellular proteases, QS signal receptor mutants have a fitness advantage over the wild type when growth is on milk protein as the sole carbon and energy source (Diggle et al., 2007; Sandoz et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Metabolic constraint is a direct benefit-based strategy of QS cheater restraint in P. aeruginosa.
source: The first is a direct benefit-based strategy called metabolic constraint (Schuster et al., 2013; Dandekar et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Quorum sensing activates genes coding for public goods (such as extracellular proteases), as well as a limited set of privately utilized goods (such as a hydrolase that allows producing cells to utilize adenosine) in P. aeruginosa.
source: Quorum sensing activates genes coding for public goods (such as extracellular proteases), as well as a limited set of privately utilized goods (such as a hydrolase that allows producing cells to utilize adenosine).
evidence: This is established knowledge about P. aeruginosa QS regulation.

claim: When cells are supplied with both casein and adenosine, QS signal receptor (LasR) mutant cheats are penalized and constrained in P. aeruginosa.
source: When cells are supplied with both casein and adenosine, QS signal receptor (LasR) mutant cheats are penalized and constrained (Dandekar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Metabolic prudence is a mechanism where the QS-controlled public good is only made when its production is not costly.
source: A second mechanism has been called metabolic prudence (Xavier et al., 2011) where the QS-controlled public good is only made when it's production is not costly.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Metabolic prudence minimizes the cost of cooperation.
source: Metabolic prudence minimizes the cost of cooperation.
evidence: This is an inference about the function of metabolic prudence.

claim: QS competent cooperators produce cyanide and are more resistant to cyanide than QS mutant cheats in P. aeruginosa, and thus the cooperators can constrain cheats by slowing their growth with cyanide.
source: QS competent cooperators produce cyanide and are more resistant to cyanide than QS mutant cheats, and thus the cooperators can constrain cheats by slowing their growth with cyanide (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The P. aeruginosa policing is a rare example of this sort of activity in bacteria.
source: The P. aeruginosa policing is a rare example of this sort of activity in bacteria
evidence: This is a statement based on knowledge of the literature.

claim: RNAseq was used to identify genes in the Burkholderia thailandensis QS regulon.
source: We recently used RNAseq to identify genes in the Burkholderia thailandensis QS regulon (Majerczyk et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: B. thailandensis has three AHL QS systems, BtaR1-I1, BtaR2-I2 and BtaR3-I3.
source: B. thailandensis has three AHL QS systems, BtaR1-I1, BtaR2-I2 and BtaR3-I3 (Ulrich et al., 2004; Chandler et al., 2009; Duerkop et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Together, the QS systems control hundreds of genes in B. thailandensis.
source: Together, the QS systems control hundreds of genes.
evidence: This is supported by the authors' previous research.

claim: The BtaR1-I1 regulon appears to be the largest as BtaR1 regulates >150 genes.
source: The BtaR1-I1 regulon appears to be the largest as BtaR1 regulates >150 genes (Majerczyk et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Expression of several genes shown to encode Type VI secretion system (T6SS) substrates, including characterized toxins and their cognate immunity or antitoxin genes, are activated by QS in B. thailandensis.
source: We queried the transcriptomics data and discovered that expression of several genes shown to encode Type VI secretion system (T6SS) substrates, including characterized toxins and their cognate immunity or antitoxin genes, are activated by QS.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of transcriptomics data from the study.

claim: Expression of a toxin and its antitoxin results in a toxin-resistant producer cell, which can deliver toxins via the secretion apparatus via cell-cell contact to a sensitive cell thereby inhibiting growth of the sensitive cell.
source: Expression of a toxin and its antitoxin results in a toxin-resistant producer cell, which can deliver toxins via the secretion apparatus via cell-cell contact to a sensitive cell thereby inhibiting growth of the sensitive cell (Russell et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about T6SS toxin-immunity systems, supported by citation.

claim: T6S provides wild-type B. thailandensis with an ability to constrain BtaR1 mutants in a contact-dependent manner.
source: We show that T6S provides wild-type B. thailandensis with an ability to constrain BtaR1 mutants in a contact-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: T6S has been shown to provide a competitive interspecies or interstrain advantage.
source: T6S has been shown to provide a competitive interspecies or interstrain advantage, and some T6Ss have been shown to play a role in bacterial virulence (Schwarz et al., 2010; 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Some T6Ss have been shown to play a role in bacterial virulence.
source: T6S has been shown to provide a competitive interspecies or interstrain advantage, and some T6Ss have been shown to play a role in bacterial virulence (Schwarz et al., 2010; 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: After 3 days in broth, the BtaR1- mutant showed an increase from 1% of the total population to 50%.
source: After 3 days in broth, the BtaR1- mutant showed an increase from 1% of the total population to 50% (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The BtaR2- and BtaR3- mutants did not have a growth advantage over the parent and remained at about 1% of the population throughout the experiment in broth coculture.
source: The BtaR2- and BtaR3- mutants did not have a growth advantage over the parent and remained at about 1% of the population throughout the experiment (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Growth rates and yields of the BtaR1- mutant and the parent in pure culture were similar with a small but reproducible difference during late logarithmic phase where the parent showed slightly slower growth than the mutant.
source: Growth rates and yields of the BtaR1- mutant and the parent in pure culture were similar with a small but reproducible difference during late logarithmic phase where the parent showed slightly slower growth than the mutant (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: At 7 hr post-inoculation in pure liquid culture, there was a reproducible and statistically significant increase in cell number for the BtaR1- mutant; the average cell yield of the wild-type parent was 1.8 x 10^9 CFU/mL and the BtaR1- mutant was 2.6 x 10^9 CFU/mL (p value=0.0041).
source: At 7 hr post-inoculation in pure liquid culture, there was a reproducible and statistically significant increase in cell number for the BtaR1- mutant; the average cell yield of the wild-type parent was 1.8 x 109 CFU/mL and the BtaR1- mutant was 2.6 x 109 CFU/mL (p value=0.0041) (Figure 1B, data for this figure can be found in the Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The slight difference in post-exponential growth rate coincides with the point during growth when QS gene expression is expected to be most evident, and when the BtaR1- mutant begins to take over the population.
source: The slight difference in post-exponential growth rate coincides with the point during growth when we expect QS gene expression to be most evident, and when the BtaR1- mutant begins to take over the population (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data and knowledge of QS timing.

claim: The slight influence on growth of the parent is attributed to the cost of BtaR1-mediated QS and QS-dependent gene expression.
source: We attribute the slight influence on growth of the parent to the cost of BtaR1-mediated QS and QS-dependent gene expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: BtaR1 controls approximately 164 genes in post-exponential phase, whereas BtaR2 and BtaR3 controlled 20 and 12, respectively.
source: Previous experiments showed that BtaR1 controls aproximately 164 genes in post-exponential phase, whereas BtaR2 and BtaR3 controlled 20 and 12, respectively (Majerczyk et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: The larger BtaR1 regulon may impart a larger burden on growth than either the smaller BtaR2 or BtaR3 regulons.
source: We suspect that the larger BtaR1 regulon may impart a larger burden on growth than either the smaller BtaR2 or BtaR3 regulons.
evidence: This is speculation based on the size of the regulons and observed growth differences.

claim: In contrast to broth cocultures where the BtaR1- mutant had a strong fitness advantage, the BtaR1- mutant had no advantage on agar plate grown cocultures at 30°C.
source: In contrast to broth cocultures where the BtaR1- mutant had a strong fitness advantage, the BtaR1- mutant had no advantage on agar plate grown cocultures at 30°C (Figure 1D) or 37°C (data not shown).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The starting and final percent of the BtaR1- mutant after four daily plate transfers (about 36 doublings in total) was 1% of the total B. thailandensis population.
source: The starting and final percent of the BtaR1- mutant after four daily plate transfers (about 36 doublings in total) was 1% of the total B. thailandensis population.
evidence: This is experimental data from agar plate competitions.

claim: The BtaR2- and BtaR3- mutants had no fitness disadvantage on agar plates, as was true for broth cocultures.
source: The BtaR2- and BtaR3- mutants had no fitness disadvantage on agar plates, as was true for broth cocultures (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Cell contact is minimal during growth in broth but does occur when cells are grown on a solid agar surface.
source: Cell contact is minimal during growth in broth but does occur when cells are grown on a solid agar surface.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial growth in different media.

claim: QS-1 activated the contact-dependent inhibition (CDI) system encoded by the cdiAIB genes.
source: We previously reported that QS-1 activated the contact-dependent inhibition (CDI) system encoded by the cdiAIB genes (Majerczyk et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: CDI does not limit the outgrowth of the BtaR1- mutant during agar-grown cocultures.
source: However, CDI does not limit the outgrowth of the BtaR1- mutant during agar-grown cocultures.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations.

claim: B. thailandensis contains five different T6SSs, at least one of which is used for interspecies competition (T6SS-1).
source: B. thailandensis contains five different T6SSs, at least one of which is used for interspecies competition (T6SS-1) (Schwarz et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The T6SS-1 comprises a pathway that delivers effector proteins to neighboring cells upon direct cell contact.
source: The T6SS-1 comprises a pathway that delivers effector proteins to neighboring cells upon direct cell contact.
evidence: This is established knowledge about T6SS-1 function.

claim: Some T6SS-1 effectors have been characterized and are toxic.
source: Some T6SS-1 effectors have been characterized and are toxic (Russell et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: B. thailandensis is immune to the toxins because it produces cognate immunity proteins.
source: B. thailandensis is immune to the toxins because it produces cognate immunity proteins (Russell et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Genes for the T6SS-1 apparatus are not QS-controlled.
source: Although genes for the T6SS-1 apparatus are not QS-controlled, we observed that QS activates nine genes for T6SS-1 substrates, as well as an additional eight that are either adjacent to a substrate gene, fall within the same gene cluster, or include a putative T6SS-1 immunity gene (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of transcriptomics data.

claim: QS activates nine genes for T6SS-1 substrates, as well as an additional eight that are either adjacent to a substrate gene, fall within the same gene cluster, or include a putative T6SS-1 immunity gene.
source: Although genes for the T6SS-1 apparatus are not QS-controlled, we observed that QS activates nine genes for T6SS-1 substrates, as well as an additional eight that are either adjacent to a substrate gene, fall within the same gene cluster, or include a putative T6SS-1 immunity gene (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of transcriptomics data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Ten of 15 genes in a cluster spanning BTH_I2691-BTH_I2705 were QS activated.
source: Ten of 15 genes in a cluster spanning BTH_I2691-BTH_I2705 were QS activated (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on transcriptomics data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: BTH_I2698 (tle1) and BTH_I2699 (tli1) are a known T6S toxin and immunity pair that code for a lipase and immunity protein.
source: Two of these 10 QS-activated genes, BTH_I2698 (tle1) and BTH_I2699 (tli1), are a known T6S toxin and immunity pair that code for a lipase and immunity protein (Russell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: When a B. thailandensis recipient cell does not produce the Tli1 immunity protein, Tle1 acts as a T6SS-1-delivered antibacterial factor.
source: When a B. thailandensis recipient cell does not produce the Tli1 immunity protein, Tle1 acts as a T6SS-1-delivered antibacterial factor (Russell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: QS activates neighboring tle1 and tli1 paralogs (BTH_I2701 and BTH_I2702).
source: In addition to tle1 and tli1, QS activates neighboring tle1 and tli1 paralogs (BTH_I2701 and BTH_I2702) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on transcriptomics data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The wild type outcompeted the T6SS-1 effector and immunity mutant.
source: Consistent with a previous publication (Russell et al., 2013), the wild type outcompeted the T6SS-1 effector and immunity mutant (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2B, consistent with previous work.

claim: The BtaR1- mutant was impaired in inhibition of the effector and immunity mutant.
source: We also found that the BtaR1- mutant was impaired in inhibition of the effector and immunity mutant (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The BtaR2- and BtaR3- mutants each showed wild-type levels of inhibition of the T6SS-1 effector and immunity mutant.
source: The BtaR2- and BtaR3- mutants each showed wild-type levels of inhibition (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The T6SS-1-mediated killing defect in the BtaR1- mutant results from its inability to fully activate expression of one or more T6S toxin genes.
source: We propose that the T6SS-1-mediated killing defect in the BtaR1- mutant results from its inability to fully activate expression of one or more T6S toxin genes.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on experimental observations.

claim: In LB agar competition experiments with a △clpV T6SS-1 secretion apparatus mutant (T6SS-1-) and a BtaR1-T6SS-1- mutant, the BtaR1-T6SS-1- mutant rose in frequency from about 1% to nearly 25% of the population.
source: In this experiment, the BtaR1-T6SS-1- mutant rose in frequency from about 1% to nearly 25% of the population (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: When the T6SS-1- mutants were complemented with clpV to restore the function of the T6SS-1 apparatus, a btaR1 mutation no longer conferred a coculture growth advantage.
source: When the T6SS-1- mutants were complemented with clpV to restore the function of the T6SS-1 apparatus, a btaR1 mutation no longer conferred a coculture growth advantage (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In broth coculture, the BtaR1- T6SS-1- mutant showed a strong fitness advantage during growth with the T6SS-1- mutant.
source: As predicted, in broth coculture, the BtaR1- T6SS-1- mutant showed a strong fitness advantage during growth with the T6SS-1- mutant (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The fitness advantage of the BtaR1- T6SS-1- mutant in broth was nearly identical to the fitness advantage of the BtaR1- mutant during coculture in broth with the wild-type parent and to a T6SS-1 complemented competition.
source: This fitness advantage was nearly identical to the fitness advantage of the BtaR1- mutant during coculture in broth with the wild-type parent (Figure 1A) and to a T6SS-1 complemented competition (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data from multiple figures.

claim: The parent, with an intact QS system, would express quorum-activated T6SS-1 toxin and immunity proteins, whereas the BtaR1- mutant should not fully induce its T6SS-1 effectors and immunity factors.
source: We reason that the parent, with an intact QS system, would express quorum-activated T6SS-1 toxin and immunity proteins, whereas the BtaR1- mutant should not fully induce its T6SS-1 effectors and immunity factors.
evidence: This is reasoning based on the experimental data and knowledge of QS regulation.

claim: The BtaR1- mutant would be sensitive to cell contact-dependent growth inhibition or killing by the wild type.
source: As such, the BtaR1- mutant would be sensitive to cell contact-dependent growth inhibition or killing by the wild type.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: QS control of T6SS-1-mediated toxicity and immunity genes allows QS competent members of B. thailandensis colonies to police against BtaR1- QS mutants.
source: We present evidence that QS control of T6SS-1-mediated toxicity and immunity genes allows QS competent members of B. thailandensis colonies to police against BtaR1- QS mutants.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: During planktonic growth in broth where T6SS-1 does not function due to limited cell contact, BtaR1- mutants have a substantial fitness advantage over wild-type cells, presumably because of the cost associated with BtaR1-dependent activities.
source: During planktonic growth in broth where T6SS-1 does not function due to limited cell contact, BtaR1- mutants have a substantial fitness advantage over wild-type cells, presumably because of the cost associated with BtaR1-dependent activities.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data with speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Policing of social deviants in Myxococcus xanthus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa has been reported previously.
source: Policing of social deviants in Myxococcus xanthus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa has been reported previously (Manhes and Velicer, 2011; Sandoz et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: B. thailandensis T6S-mediated killing is active against Proteobacteria species other than B. thailandensis and is thought to be important for interspecies competition.
source: B. thailandensis T6S-mediated killing is active against Proteobacteria species other than B. thailandensis and is thought to be important for interspecies competition (Schwarz et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: T6Ss occur in many species of Proteobacteria where they can provide an advantage over competing species.
source: T6Ss occur in many species of Proteobacteria where they can provide an advantage over competing species (see Russell et al., 2014 for review).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to a review.

claim: In other organisms including Pectobacterium atrosepticum, P. aeruginosa, Aeromonas hydrophila, Yersinia pseudotuberculosis, Chromobacterium violaceum, Vibrio cholerae, Vibrio alginolyticus, and Vibrio parahaemolyticus, QS regulates genes for the T6S apparatus.
source: We note that in other organisms including, Pectobacterium atrosepticum (Liu et al., 2008), P. aeruginosa (Lesic et al., 2009), Aeromonas hydrophila (Khajanchi et al., 2009), Yersinia pseudotuberculosis (Zhang et al., 2011), Chromobacterium violaceum (Stauff and Bassler, 2011), Vibrio cholerae (Zheng et al., 2010), Vibrio alginolyticus, (Sheng et al., 2012), and Vibrio parahaemolyticus (Wang et al., 2013), QS regulates genes for the T6S apparatus (not the effector and immunity factors as we describe for B. thailandensis).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: QS regulation of the T6S apparatus might play a role in policing QS mutants during polymicrobial competitions or in other scenarios where T6S might benefit the producing cell.
source: We suspect QS regulation of the T6S apparatus might play a role in policing QS mutants during polymicrobial competitions or in other scenarios where T6S might benefit the producing cell.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings of the study.

claim: Other types of toxin-antitoxin systems have been reported to be under control of other non-AHL-mediated quorum sensing systems.
source: Furthermore, we note that other types of toxin-antitoxin systems have been reported to be under control of other non-AHL-mediated quorum sensing systems, for example the E. coli mazEF encoded toxin-antitoxin genes are controlled by a linear pentapeptide quorum sensing signal (Kolodkin-Gal et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The E. coli mazEF encoded toxin-antitoxin genes are controlled by a linear pentapeptide quorum sensing signal.
source: Furthermore, we note that other types of toxin-antitoxin systems have been reported to be under control of other non-AHL-mediated quorum sensing systems, for example the E. coli mazEF encoded toxin-antitoxin genes are controlled by a linear pentapeptide quorum sensing signal (Kolodkin-Gal et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Under the conditions of the experiments the BtaR1-BtaI1 QS system carries with it a metabolic cost, which is evident in broth culture competition experiments and to a lesser extent in pure broth culture growth curves.
source: Under the conditions of our experiments the BtaR1-BtaI1 QS system carries with it a metabolic cost, which is evident in broth culture competition experiments and to a lesser extent in pure broth culture grow curves.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data.

claim: The BtaR2-BtaI2 and BtaR3-BtaI3 QS systems do not appear to carry this large cost.
source: The BtaR2-BtaI2 and BtaR3-BtaI3 QS systems do not appear to carry this large cost.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing no fitness disadvantage for these mutants.

claim: Wild-type populations can mitigate the cost of BtaR1-BtaI1 gene regulation by hindering the growth of QS mutants via regulation of cell-contact-dependent toxin and immunity proteins.
source: We describe a mechanism by which wild-type populations can mitigate the cost of BtaR1-BtaI1 gene regulation by hindering the growth of QS mutants via regulation of cell-contact-dependent toxin and immunity proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: QS-proficient bacteria are outcompeted in populations of signal blind non-cooperators in the absence of the T6S cell-contact growth inhibition system.
source: This is a form of microbial policing; QS-proficient bacteria are outcompeted in populations of signal blind non-cooperators in the absence of the T6S cell-contact growth inhibition system.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data.

claim: BtaR1 promotes aggregation of cells under some conditions.
source: It is interesting that BtaR1 also promotes aggregation of cells under some conditions (Chandler et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The BtaR1 system brings cells into close proximity where they can resist infiltration by other strains and species while at the same time protect themselves against social deviant BtaR1 mutant bacteria.
source: One can imagine that this system brings cells into close proximity where they can resist infiltration by other strains and species while at the same time protect themselves against social deviant BtaR1 mutant bacteria (Figure 4).
evidence: This is speculation about the integrated function of the system.
